narrative:
The model estimated a 64.9% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That does not mean failure is certain, but it was high enough that the admissions decision treated it as a major risk, so your application was rejected.

The strongest factor behind that prediction was your third-year class-rank decile: you are in decile 1, far below the accepted-student average of about 5.8. This was the top factor and it pushed strongly toward predicted bar-exam failure. The second most influential factor was your family income bracket. Being in the middle-income group was a modest plus, pushing slightly toward passing, and it matches a common profile among accepted students, but it was not enough to outweigh the academic concerns. The third most important factor was your LSAT score of 22.70, well below the accepted-student average of 37.18; this also pushed the prediction toward failure. Your first-year decile and undergraduate GPA point in the same direction, though they were not among the top three drivers in this explanation.

To move forward, ask admissions whether the prediction was decisive and what appeal or reconsideration process exists. If you reapply, focus on raising your LSAT score and building a record of stronger academic performance, and seek advising on how to demonstrate bar-exam readiness.
